title: Render and re-render
summary: Rendering is React calling your component function to calculate what the UI should look like.
whenToUse: Understand this when debugging why a component updates, why console logs run again, or why a value appears stale during an event.
do: Think of render as a calculation from props and state to JSX.
Expect a component to re-render when its state changes.
Keep render logic pure so calling the component again is safe.
dont: Do not treat a render as the same thing as changing the real DOM.
Do not perform side effects directly while rendering.

codeSnippets.title: UI is calculated from state
codeSnippets.description: When state changes, React calls the component again and recalculates the JSX.
codeSnippets.explanation: Clicking the button updates state. React calls Counter again, so the log runs again with the new value.

commonMistake: Assuming a re-render means React recreated the whole DOM instead of recalculating the component output first.
interviewQuestion: What does it mean when a React component renders?
interviewAnswer: React calls the component function to calculate JSX from the current props and state. React then decides what DOM work is actually needed.

title: State update batching
summary: React can group multiple state updates from the same event before rendering once.
whenToUse: Understand batching when multiple setter calls happen in one handler and the UI updates after the handler finishes.
do: Use functional updates when the next state depends on the previous state.
Remember that state variables inside the current handler do not change immediately.
Group related updates in the same event handler when they describe one user action.
dont: Do not expect a state variable to change immediately after calling its setter.
Do not repeat setState(value + 1) when each update depends on the previous result.

codeSnippets.title: Increment three times safely
codeSnippets.description: Functional updates receive the latest pending state value.
codeSnippets.explanation: Each updater receives the latest queued value, so one click adds three instead of repeating the same stale value.

commonMistake: Calling setCount(count + 1) multiple times in one handler and expecting each call to see a new count.
interviewQuestion: Why are functional state updates useful?
interviewAnswer: They are useful when the next state depends on the previous state, especially when React batches multiple updates together.

courseReference.notes: The tabs demo contrasts repeated stale updates with functional updates.

title: State as a snapshot
summary: During one render, props and state behave like a snapshot that event handlers close over.
whenToUse: Use this model when a console log after setState still shows the old value or a delayed callback reads an older value.
do: Treat state values inside one render as fixed.
Use functional updates when delayed or repeated work depends on previous state.
Pass the exact value needed into async callbacks when possible.
dont: Do not assume calling a setter mutates the current state variable.
Do not debug state by only logging immediately after a setter call.

codeSnippets.title: The current handler sees old state
codeSnippets.description: A setter schedules the next render; it does not rewrite the current variable.
codeSnippets.explanation: The log prints the likes value from the render that created this handler. The reset appears in the next render.

commonMistake: Thinking setState changes the current local variable instead of scheduling a new render with a new value.
interviewQuestion: Why can state look stale right after calling a setter?
interviewAnswer: The handler is using the state snapshot from the current render. The setter schedules a new render where the updated value will be available.

title: Component identity and state preservation
summary: React preserves state for a component while it keeps the same type in the same position in the UI tree.
whenToUse: Use this to understand why switching visible content may keep state, or why replacing one component with a different one resets state.
do: Think about component type and position in the tree.
Expect state to be preserved when React sees the same component in the same place.
Use different component types when switching views should naturally reset their state.
dont: Do not assume hiding and showing always resets state.
Do not rely on visual position alone; React tracks identity in the rendered tree.

codeSnippets.title: Same component position keeps state
codeSnippets.description: React keeps Panel state while the same component type remains in the same tree position.
codeSnippets.explanation: Changing item does not reset isOpen because Panel is still the same component in the same position.

commonMistake: Expecting a component's state to reset just because its props changed.
interviewQuestion: When does React preserve a component's state?
interviewAnswer: React preserves state when the same component type remains in the same position of the rendered tree.

courseReference.project: How React Works Behind the Scenes
courseReference.notes: The tab demo shows state being preserved while the same tab content component stays in position.

title: Resetting state with key
summary: Changing a component's key tells React to treat it as a different component and reset its state.
whenToUse: Use a key to intentionally reset form fields, tab content, detail panels, or any component state when the selected data changes.
do: Use a stable meaningful key when you intentionally want a fresh component instance.
Use keys to separate state between different selected records.
Keep the key tied to identity, such as an id or slug.
dont: Do not use random keys because they reset state on every render.
Do not add keys blindly to fix unrelated bugs.

codeSnippets.title: Reset details when selection changes
codeSnippets.description: A changing key creates a fresh Details component for each selected item.
codeSnippets.explanation: When selectedId changes, React discards the old Details state and mounts a new Details component.

commonMistake: Using a random key, which forces React to throw away state every render.
interviewQuestion: How can a key reset component state?
interviewAnswer: A different key changes the component's identity, so React unmounts the old instance and mounts a new one with fresh state.

courseReference.project: How React Works Behind the Scenes
courseReference.notes: The final tabs demo uses a key on tab content so each selected tab can get fresh state.

title: Component vs React element
summary: A component is a function you define; a React element is the object created when JSX describes that component or a DOM tag.
whenToUse: Use this distinction when learning why components must be capitalized, why JSX is not HTML, and what React receives from your render.
do: Use JSX to create React elements.
Think of elements as descriptions, not DOM nodes.
dont: Do not call component functions directly in normal app code.
Do not confuse a JSX element with the real browser DOM element.

codeSnippets.title: JSX creates an element description
codeSnippets.description: A component function and an element are related but not the same thing.
codeSnippets.explanation: Greeting is the component function. element is a React element that describes rendering Greeting with a name prop.

commonMistake: Thinking JSX immediately creates DOM nodes instead of React element descriptions.
interviewQuestion: What is the difference between a component and a React element?
interviewAnswer: A component is a function or class that describes UI. A React element is the lightweight description produced by JSX and used by React during rendering.
